profiles.identity_context:
Andrew Jacob Spisak was born 1886 in Rozgony, Austria-Hungary (present-day Rozhanovce, Slovakia). Immigrated to the United States in 1904.

Born 1886, Rozgony, Austria-Hungary (present-day Rozhanovce, Slovakia). Metalworker; sign painter. Migrated to US 1904. 1912 lost his left eye and suffered a skull fracture from a workplace accident. Communist Party of America. Braddock, Pennsylvania. Arrested April 29, 1921 by members of the Edgar Thomson Steel Company’s private police force for posting radical May Day leaflets published by the United Communist Party; convicted of violating Pennsylvania’s sedition law, then turned over to immigration authorities. Released November 1922; detained again June 1923 and held on Ellis Island for seventeen months while awaiting a passport from Czechoslovakia, which was initially denied on the grounds that he had resided outside of Czechoslovakian territory for more than ten years and therefore lost his citizenship. Deported to Czechoslovakia, October 24, 1924.

INS file 54809/601; FBI file BS 202600-1897

profiles.name: Arthur Taylor
profiles.identity_context: Arthur Taylor was a United Mine Workers of America organizer in the District 2 campaign that swept Somerset County, Pennsylvania, in the great 1922 coal strike. In April 1922, as the county's non-union miners prepared to walk out, he was arrested at Somerset alongside fellow organizer Powers Hapgood — a contemporary account in the New Majority records the two as having been in custody there two days before the successful April 17 organizing action at Boswell, which places the arrest around April 15, 1922. Both men were free again in time for the Boswell action, so the detention lasted at most about two days, most likely a brief hold or a single overnight stay. The charge wording and disposition have not survived in the accessible record; the fuller story of the Somerset arrests awaits the organizing telegrams preserved in the UMWA District 2 papers at Indiana University of Pennsylvania.

profiles.name: J. A. Casdorf
profiles.query: "J. A. Casdorf" IWW prison 1922 portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: J. A. Casdorf was an IWW member from Sacramento. J. A. Casdorf received a five-year prison sentence, which he served in San Quentin from May 6, 1922, to December 5, 1923. Along with codefendant Earl Firey, Casdorf was charged with the crime of being a member of the IWW, an organization that illegally advocated "criminal syndicalism." After the defendants' first two witnesses (P. Beasley and Charles B. La Rue) testified, the witnesses were promptly arrested under the California criminal syndicalism law. Thereafter the prosecuting state attorney declared in the presence of other potential witnesses that "all witnesses who would thereafter take the stand in this case and admit they were paid up members of the IWW in good standing, would be arrested." The defense pleaded that such statements by the prosecution were prejudicial, that "other witnesses" were "intimidated and terrorized so as to render them less efficient as witnesses" and that other prospective witnesses were "scared away." The trial judge overruled these objections, and eventually eight other IWW members who took the stand were arrested. On appeal, the California District Court of Appeals affirmed Casdorf s conviction. The court held that the "propriety" of the district attorney's action was "debatable, " but that he "acted in good faith" merely to "warn" witnesses of the "consequence[s]" of their testimony. The court held that there was "no prejudice to the substantial rights of the defendants." After the Casdorf conviction, the ten witnesses who took the stand on his behalf were all tried and convicted under the criminal syndicalism law. These convictions were also upheld in People v. LaRue, 216 P. 627 (Cal. App. 1923).
profiles.finding: Identity-specific portrait search completed using deportation/prison/affiliation context. No adequately identified usable real image verified. Results indexed by query group; research remains unresolved.

profiles.name: Louis Allen
profiles.identity_context:
Louis Allen was a Los Angeles member of the Industrial Workers of the World, convicted with eight co-defendants under California's Criminal Syndicalism Act and sentenced to an indeterminate term of one to fourteen years. He was imprisoned at Folsom State Prison from December 1921 as prisoner number 12026.

A scholarly history records that guards at Folsom covered his head with a blanket, dragged him from solitary confinement and beat him unconscious, and that complaints were filed with the prison board.

His release date is in conflict by one day. A compilation gives September 11, 1925, while a contemporary newspaper report of September 11 says the release would happen "tomorrow", which would make it September 12. The compilation date is recorded and the conflict is noted rather than silently resolved.

This was a state prosecution. An earlier version of this record classified it as a federal Espionage or Sedition Act case.

The June 1925 labor-press political-prisoner birthday notice lists him at Folsom Prison, Represa, under prisoner number 12026 — matching the number already recorded here — with a June 22 birthday (no birth year is given).

profiles.name: Mayer Libson Nehring
profiles.query: "Mayer Libson Nehring" deportee 1921 radical portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context:
Mayer Libson Nehring was born 1892 in Warsaw, Russia (present-day Poland). Worked as a hatmaker, chiropractor, pharmacist. Immigrated to the United States in 1914.

Anarchist and IWW organizer in Cleveland. In February 1919 he was convicted under the Espionage Act for an antiwar speech and sentenced to nineteen years. At his sentencing the judge declared: “I presume that the Russian Bolshevists would welcome you, and Lenine and Trotzky would be glad to see you back in the event that the government should deport you…in the event that the Government does not send you back to Russia I am going to protect America from your activities by sending you the Atlanta penitentiary for 19 years at hard labor.” His sentence was later commuted on condition of deportation, and he was deported February 26, 1921.

Refused entry at Libau because of anarchism, he coauthored An Open Letter to the Russian Premier Lenin and returned to the U.S., where he apparently ceased radical activity. He received an unconditional presidential pardon in September 1930. In 1935 he applied for US citizenship and was denied, but the decision was reversed on appeal.

profiles.name: Sam Povff
profiles.identity_context:
Sam Povff was born 1878 in Poltava, Russia (present-day Ukraine). Immigrated to the United States in 1910.

An anarchist since age 17. Arrested in 1899 for revolutionary activities but released. Later claimed he participated in a mutiny at the Kronstadt naval base and was sentenced to 13 years’ internal exile in Siberia, from which he escaped. 

In the United States he briefly belonged to an anarchist organization in New York, then moved to the West Coast where he used numerous aliases and supported himself through apparently politically motivated theft. Arrested 1911 in Huntington, Oregon for larceny (receiving a two-year sentence); circa 1912 in Stockton for burglary (two years in San Quentin State Prison); and 1914 in Los Angeles for highway robbery (a six-year sentence, of which he served four years and two months). Arrested again in Portland in 1919 for attempted robbery of moonshine sellers, explaining “They had no right to poison the working class people. I think I had a right to rob them.” Immigration authorities called him “a most reprehensible and undesirable character.” Deported to Russia December 17, 1922.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

Around forty-nine men were convicted of conspiracy; Teddy Arunsky was sentenced to 10 years. The ILD's Labor Defender profiled the Cliftonville prisoners in October 1926, shortly before most of the group were released. The spelling of the miners' names follows that source.

profiles.name: Vincent George Tryzno
profiles.query: "Vincent George Tryzno" deportee 1921 radical portrait photograph
profiles.identity_context: Vincent George Tryzno was a Polish tailor born in 1880 in Wojstom in the Russian Empire, in present-day Belarus. He immigrated to Baltimore in 1899, filed a declaration of intention to become a citizen in 1906, and later belonged to the Industrial Workers of the World, the Amalgamated Clothing Workers of America, and the Baltimore Union of Russian Workers. He served for six months as treasurer of the local Russian workers’ group. Department of Justice agents arrested Tryzno on November 7, 1919, and held him in the Baltimore City Jail. At deportation hearings on November 13 and November 25, he denied being an anarchist and disputed the government’s claim that his local union was controlled by the national Union of Russian Workers. The federal government ultimately deported him on February 26, 1921.

profiles.name: Vincenzo Frattesi
profiles.identity_context:
Vincenzo Frattesi was born 1886 in Pergola, Italy. Immigrated to the United States in 1913.

Emigrated to Avignon, France, where he was fined for assault in 1908, and was jailed for eight days in 1910 for the same offense. After immigrating to the United States in 1913, he became active in Milwaukee’s anarchist Circolo Studi Sociali, along with his siblings and brother-in-law. Following the 1917 Milwaukee anarchist “riot,” convicted as an accessory to the attempted murder of a police officer and sentenced to twenty-five years in prison, a conviction upheld by the Wisconsin Supreme Court. While incarcerated, repeatedly disciplined for infractions and in 1920 was declared insane and transferred to a mental hospital. Pardoned in 1922 on condition of deportation and deported on February 25, 1922.

Upon arrival in Italy, institutionalized in Naples as “paranoid” and released in November 1924. Later settled in Fossombrone, where he remained under surveillance and continued to express anarchist beliefs. In July 1928 he was recommitted to a psychiatric hospital in Pesaro and diagnosed with “paranoid early dementia.” Remained institutionalized as of 1940.

Adapted from Kenyon Zimmer, Red Scare Deportees (kenyonzimmer.com), compiled from INS deportation case files.

profiles.identity_context: Witte Moses Shakman was a Jewish tailor born in 1882 in Odesa in the Russian Empire, in present-day Ukraine. He immigrated to the United States in 1915 and lived in Chicago with his wife Rachael and their daughter Lucy. Shakman had belonged to the Russian Federation of the Socialist Party and later joined the Communist Party, the United Communist Party, the Industrial Workers of the World, and the Amalgamated Clothing Workers. Federal authorities arrested him in Chicago and deported him to Russia on March 18, 1921.
